Working Title: Which Planet Has a Day Longer Than Its Year?
Hook (0-2 sec): One planet finishes a year before it finishes one rotation. Guess which one.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Show Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter; pause 2.5 seconds.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Venus. One rotation takes about 243 Earth days, while one orbit takes about 225 days.
Core Explanation: Venus rotates extremely slowly and in the opposite direction to most planets. Distinguish a sidereal rotation from sunrise-to-sunrise time.
Final Wow Fact: On Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
Accuracy / Caveat: Say rotation day, not ordinary solar day; sunrise-to-sunrise is about 117 Earth days.

Working Title: Which Planet Could Float in Water?
Hook (0-2 sec): If a planet-sized ocean existed, which planet would float?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Show Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; ask viewers to choose.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Saturn, because its average density is lower than liquid water.
Core Explanation: Average density compares total mass with total volume. Saturn has no solid surface and the ocean is only a thought experiment.
Final Wow Fact: Saturn is the only planet in our solar system with an average density below water.
Supporting Tools: Remotion, fluid shader, SVG density gauge
Accuracy / Caveat: Clearly call this a scale-impossible thought experiment; Saturn is a gas giant without a solid surface.

Working Title: Which Planet Has the Shortest Day?
Hook (0-2 sec): Which planet spins through a full day in under ten hours?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Race all eight planets using rotation clocks.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Jupiter, with a rotation period of about 9.9 hours.
Core Explanation: A shorter rotation period means faster spinning. Jupiter spins so quickly that it bulges at its equator.
Final Wow Fact: Jupiter is more than 11 times wider than Earth yet rotates in less than half an Earth day.
Accuracy / Caveat: Gas giants rotate differentially; use the standard quoted rotation period.

Working Title: Which Planet Has the Fastest Winds?
Hook (0-2 sec): These winds can outrun the speed of sound. Which planet has them?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Neptune, where winds exceed 1,200 mph or about 2,000 km/h.
Core Explanation: Despite receiving little sunlight, Neptune has powerful atmospheric dynamics driven partly by internal heat.
Final Wow Fact: Neptune is the farthest major planet from the Sun, yet it is the solar system’s windiest world.
Accuracy / Caveat: Use “measured winds” and avoid claiming every location constantly reaches the maximum.

Working Title: What If the Sun Disappeared Right Now?
Hook (0-2 sec): For eight minutes, Earth would not notice anything. Then everything changes.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers what arrives first: darkness or loss of gravity.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Both effects would reach Earth after roughly eight minutes because changes in gravity and light propagate at light speed.
Core Explanation: Earth would then continue along a tangent rather than orbiting the missing Sun; temperatures would fall over time, not instantly.
Final Wow Fact: The last sunlight and the last gravitational influence would effectively arrive together.
Supporting Tools: Remotion timeline, particle lighting, SVG tangent path
Accuracy / Caveat: Explicitly label this as an impossible magical thought experiment; the Sun cannot simply vanish.

Working Title: How Many Earths Fit Inside the Sun?
Hook (0-2 sec): Is it ten thousand, one hundred thousand, or more than a million?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Show three answer buttons and fill the Sun with Earth spheres.
Correct Answer / Reveal: About 1.3 million Earths by volume, ignoring packing gaps.
Core Explanation: The Sun is about 109 Earth diameters wide; volume scales with the cube of diameter.
Final Wow Fact: The Sun contains more than 99% of the mass in the entire solar system.
Accuracy / Caveat: Clarify that 1.3 million is a volume ratio; real spheres leave packing gaps.

Working Title: The Planet Where It May Rain Glass Sideways
Hook (0-2 sec): This blue planet may have glass rain moving sideways at thousands of miles per hour.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the blue colour means oceans, ice, gas or silicate clouds.
Correct Answer / Reveal: HD 189733 b. Its colour likely comes from silicate particles, and models suggest glass-like rain driven sideways by extreme winds.
Core Explanation: It is a hot Jupiter exoplanet, not an Earth-like ocean world. The rain description is an interpretation of silicate weather, not direct footage.
Final Wow Fact: Its winds may reach about 5,400 mph, around seven times the speed of sound.
Supporting Tools: GPU particles, Remotion labels, MuAPI background texture
Accuracy / Caveat: Use “may” or “possibly”; the weather is inferred from observations and models.

Working Title: What Is the Coldest Known Natural Place?
Hook (0-2 sec): It is colder than the leftover glow of the Big Bang.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer Antarctica, Pluto, deep space and the Boomerang Nebula.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The Boomerang Nebula, with regions near 1 kelvin.
Core Explanation: Rapidly expanding gas cools exceptionally efficiently, dropping below the 2.7 K cosmic microwave background.
Final Wow Fact: It is around 5,000 light-years away and formed around a dying Sun-like star.
Accuracy / Caveat: Say coldest known natural region/object; laboratories can produce lower temperatures.

Working Title: How Much Would You Weigh on Other Planets?
Hook (0-2 sec): A 70-kilogram person would feel very different on Mars and Jupiter.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Let viewers choose where they would weigh least and most.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Among the planets, Mercury and Mars give about 38% of Earth weight; Jupiter gives about 2.5 times Earth weight at the reference level.
Core Explanation: Mass stays the same; weight changes with surface gravity. Gas giants lack a solid surface, so values use a reference level.
Final Wow Fact: On Saturn, despite its huge mass, the reference gravity is only slightly stronger than Earth’s.
Accuracy / Caveat: Explain reference gravity on gas giants and distinguish mass from weight.

Working Title: Can Sound Travel Through Space?
Hook (0-2 sec): Movies give space explosions a roar. Would you actually hear one?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Play an explosion twice and ask which version is physically correct.
Correct Answer / Reveal: In a vacuum, sound cannot travel because there is no material medium to carry the pressure wave.
Core Explanation: Light and radio are electromagnetic waves and can cross a vacuum; sound can travel inside spacecraft or through gas and plasma.
Final Wow Fact: An object can still vibrate in space, but without nearby matter the vibration does not become audible sound for a distant listener.
Accuracy / Caveat: Space is not perfectly empty everywhere; sound-like pressure waves can occur in gas or plasma, but ordinary audio does not cross a vacuum.

Working Title: Which Part of Your Body Has No Blood Vessels?
Hook (0-2 sec): One transparent body tissue stays alive without a single blood vessel.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer cornea, fingernail, eardrum and tooth enamel.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The cornea. It receives oxygen from tears and the air, and nutrients from surrounding fluids and tissues.
Core Explanation: Its lack of vessels helps keep it transparent for vision. The cornea is richly supplied with nerves despite being avascular.
Final Wow Fact: The cornea is one of the most densely innervated tissues in the body.
Accuracy / Caveat: Say the healthy cornea is normally avascular; disease or injury can cause abnormal vessel growth.

Working Title: How Much Blood Does Your Heart Pump in One Day?
Hook (0-2 sec): Is it enough to fill a bathtub, a tanker, or a swimming pool?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Show three container-size guesses.
Correct Answer / Reveal: About 2,000 US gallons, roughly 7,500 litres, per day for an average heart.
Core Explanation: The number comes from cardiac output accumulated across tens of thousands of beats; it varies with body size and activity.
Final Wow Fact: Over a 70-year lifetime, the heart can beat more than 2.5 billion times.
Accuracy / Caveat: Present as an average estimate, not an identical amount for everyone.

Working Title: Which Organ Can Regrow After Major Damage?
Hook (0-2 sec): One organ can restore its mass even after a large portion is removed.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer lung, kidney, liver and pancreas.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The liver. Remaining tissue enlarges and cells proliferate to restore functional mass.
Core Explanation: The removed lobe does not grow back like a salamander limb; the remaining liver compensates and regains volume.
Final Wow Fact: The liver can recover from major loss, but repeated or severe disease can overwhelm this ability.
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid saying it regrows perfectly from any damage or that 90% removal is safe in humans.

Working Title: Why Can’t You Tickle Yourself?
Hook (0-2 sec): Your fingers make the same movement, but your brain turns down the sensation.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers whether the cause is skin, nerves, prediction or strength.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Prediction. The brain anticipates the sensory result of self-generated movement and attenuates it.
Core Explanation: Motor commands produce an internal prediction; when expected and actual touch match, somatosensory activity is reduced.
Final Wow Fact: Adding a delay between your movement and the touch can make self-produced stimulation feel more ticklish.
Supporting Tools: Remotion brain overlays, SVG neural pathways
Accuracy / Caveat: Ticklishness is multifactorial; prediction and self-generated sensory attenuation are central, not the only influences.

Working Title: What Happens Inside Your Face When You Blush?
Hook (0-2 sec): Embarrassment can redirect visible blood flow before you can stop it.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the red colour comes from heat, hormones, muscle tension or widened vessels.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Facial blood vessels dilate and more blood becomes visible near the skin surface.
Core Explanation: Blushing involves autonomic nervous-system responses and is concentrated in highly visible facial, ear, neck and upper-chest vasculature.
Final Wow Fact: A blush often becomes visible seconds after the emotional trigger, even though the reaction is involuntary.
Supporting Tools: Canvas blood particles, Remotion thermal overlay
Accuracy / Caveat: Physiology is complex; avoid presenting one single pathway as fully settled.

Working Title: How Fast Can a Nerve Signal Travel?
Hook (0-2 sec): Some nerve signals can cross your body faster than a race car.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to rank walking speed, cheetah, race car and fast myelinated nerve signal.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Fast myelinated nerve fibres can conduct signals at roughly 100–120 metres per second.
Core Explanation: Speed depends on axon diameter and myelination; not all nerve signals travel this fast.
Final Wow Fact: Myelin lets the electrical impulse jump between nodes in saltatory conduction.
Supporting Tools: Remotion speed race, Canvas electrical glow
Accuracy / Caveat: Use “up to” or “fast fibres”; slower nerves can conduct far below this speed.

Working Title: Is Bone Stronger Than Steel?
Hook (0-2 sec): You have probably heard that bone is stronger than steel. Is that actually true?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to choose: absolutely yes, absolutely no, or only by strength-to-weight.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Steel is generally stronger in absolute terms, but bone has an impressive strength-to-weight ratio and is a living, self-repairing composite.
Core Explanation: The comparison depends on tension, compression, specimen direction and whether strength is normalised by mass or density.
Final Wow Fact: Bone combines stiffness, toughness, low weight and biological repair—properties a simple steel bar does not share.
Accuracy / Caveat: Never use a single “bone is five times stronger” claim without specifying the test and material grade.

Working Title: Why Do Fingers Wrinkle in Water?
Hook (0-2 sec): Your skin is not simply soaking up water—the nervous system actively creates the wrinkles.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the cause is swelling, shrinking blood vessels, cold skin or trapped air.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Small blood vessels constrict under autonomic control, pulling the fingertip surface into wrinkles.
Core Explanation: Some studies suggest wrinkles improve handling of wet objects, but results are mixed, so present the grip benefit as a supported hypothesis rather than settled fact.
Final Wow Fact: Abnormal wrinkling can be used as a clue to autonomic nerve function.
Accuracy / Caveat: Grip advantage evidence is mixed; distinguish mechanism from proposed function.

Working Title: What 24 Hours Without Sleep Does to Your Brain
Hook (0-2 sec): After one sleepless night, attention and reaction time can fall before you realise it.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to predict which changes first: memory, mood, reaction or hunger.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Multiple systems change: vigilance and reaction time worsen, mood becomes less stable, and memory formation is impaired.
Core Explanation: Effects differ by person and task; sleep deprivation is not equivalent to a fixed blood-alcohol level for everyone.
Final Wow Fact: Microsleeps can occur for seconds while the person appears awake.
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid medical diagnosis and avoid a universal alcohol-equivalence claim.

Working Title: Can Stomach Acid Dissolve Metal?
Hook (0-2 sec): Your stomach acid is powerful—but could it dissolve a metal object?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Show coin, aluminium foil, steel screw and food; ask what changes first.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Acid can corrode some metals, but the result depends on the metal, protective coatings, concentration and time. The stomach is not an instant metal-dissolving chamber.
Core Explanation: Gastric acid is mainly hydrochloric acid at low pH, but swallowed metal objects remain dangerous and require medical attention.
Final Wow Fact: The stomach protects itself with mucus, bicarbonate and rapidly renewed lining cells.
Accuracy / Caveat: Do not give ingestion instructions; include a clear “do not test—seek medical care” warning.

Working Title: Which Animal Has Three Hearts?
Hook (0-2 sec): Two hearts serve the gills, and one serves the rest of the body.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer shark, octopus, dolphin and crab.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The octopus and other cephalopods have three hearts.
Core Explanation: Two branchial hearts send oxygen-poor blood through the gills; the systemic heart pumps oxygenated blood to the body.
Final Wow Fact: Their blood is blue because the oxygen carrier hemocyanin contains copper.
Accuracy / Caveat: Say cephalopods generally; avoid implying every heart beats identically in every activity state.

Working Title: Which Animal Survived Exposure to Space?
Hook (0-2 sec): This animal endured vacuum and radiation outside a spacecraft.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer ant, tardigrade, cockroach and jellyfish.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Tardigrades. In experiments, some survived direct exposure to the space vacuum, especially when shielded from intense ultraviolet radiation.
Core Explanation: They enter a desiccated tun state that greatly reduces metabolism; survival does not mean they live normally or indefinitely in space.
Final Wow Fact: They were the first animals shown to survive direct exposure to outer space.
Supporting Tools: Remotion quiz, particle radiation, microscope view
Accuracy / Caveat: Do not claim all tardigrades survive all space conditions; UV exposure reduced survival.

Working Title: Why Is Horseshoe Crab Blood Blue?
Hook (0-2 sec): This blue blood has helped test medicines and medical devices for bacterial contamination.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the blue colour comes from copper, seawater, bacteria or pigment.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Copper-containing hemocyanin carries oxygen and makes the blood blue.
Core Explanation: Amoebocyte cells in the blood react strongly to bacterial endotoxins, historically enabling highly sensitive contamination tests.
Final Wow Fact: Horseshoe crabs are more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs.
Accuracy / Caveat: Mention conservation concerns and synthetic alternatives; do not frame harvesting as harmless.

Working Title: Which Animal Sees Colours Humans Cannot?
Hook (0-2 sec): This animal detects ultraviolet light and patterns of polarisation invisible to us.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer eagle, cat, mantis shrimp and dolphin.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Mantis shrimp have specialised photoreceptors that detect ultraviolet and polarised light.
Core Explanation: More receptor types do not automatically mean “better colour vision”; their neural processing differs from ours.
Final Wow Fact: Some mantis shrimp can judge distance using a single eye.
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid repeating exaggerated claims that they see every imaginable colour or infrared as established fact.

Working Title: Which Living Animal Has the Strongest Measured Bite?
Hook (0-2 sec): The record bite can deliver more than 16,000 newtons of force.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Rank lion, great white shark, hippopotamus and saltwater crocodile.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The saltwater crocodile holds the highest directly measured bite force among living animals in a major comparative study.
Core Explanation: Bite force varies with body size and measurement method; shark estimates are often modelled rather than directly measured.
Final Wow Fact: Crocodilians combine extreme closing force with relatively weak jaw-opening muscles.
Accuracy / Caveat: Use “strongest directly measured in the study,” not a timeless universal claim across every species and method.

Working Title: How Do Geckos Walk on Ceilings?
Hook (0-2 sec): No glue, no suction cups—millions of microscopic hairs create the grip.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the mechanism is suction, sticky liquid, tiny claws or intermolecular forces.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Microscopic setae branch into nanoscale contacts that get close enough for van der Waals attractions to add up.
Core Explanation: Geckos control attachment directionally by changing the angle of their toe hairs, allowing rapid release.
Final Wow Fact: The system can adhere to many smooth materials without leaving sticky residue.
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid saying van der Waals forces alone explain every condition; surface roughness and mechanics matter.

Working Title: Which Animal Can Regrow Limbs and Parts of Its Brain?
Hook (0-2 sec): This salamander can rebuild structures that humans replace with scar tissue.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer lizard, axolotl, frog and octopus.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The axolotl can regenerate limbs, spinal cord, parts of the heart and parts of the central nervous system.
Core Explanation: After injury, cells form a blastema that grows and re-patterns the missing structure.
Final Wow Fact: Regeneration restores complex tissues in the correct arrangement, not just a simple stump.
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid saying unlimited perfect regeneration; capacity can decline under repeated injury and varies by tissue.

Working Title: Why Don’t Woodpeckers Get Concussions?
Hook (0-2 sec): Their skulls may not be shock absorbers at all.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the protection comes from spongy skulls, a tiny brain, soft beak or slow impacts.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Recent research suggests the head acts more like a stiff hammer; small brain size and impact conditions keep pressures below damaging thresholds.
Core Explanation: Older shock-absorber explanations are oversimplified, and repeated impacts may still carry biological costs.
Final Wow Fact: A shock-absorbing skull would reduce the efficiency of pecking into wood.
Accuracy / Caveat: Present as updated evidence, not final certainty for every species and impact condition.

Working Title: How Can Ants Carry Many Times Their Weight?
Hook (0-2 sec): An ant can lift loads that would be impossible at human scale.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the advantage comes from stronger muscle, small size, six legs or all three.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Small size changes the scaling: muscle force relates to cross-sectional area, while body mass grows with volume. Multiple legs and exoskeleton design also help.
Core Explanation: Exact carrying multiples vary widely by species and task; avoid one universal number.
Final Wow Fact: As animals get smaller, their strength relative to body weight generally increases.
Accuracy / Caveat: Use “many times” or species-specific tested values; do not claim every ant carries 50 times its weight.

Working Title: Can a Cockroach Live Without Its Head?
Hook (0-2 sec): The body can keep moving for days—but not because it is immortal.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask how it breathes without a mouth or nose.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Cockroaches breathe through spiracles along the body and have distributed nerve centres, so basic movement can continue after decapitation.
Core Explanation: They eventually die from dehydration, starvation, infection or fluid loss; the head may also show reflex activity briefly.
Final Wow Fact: Their open circulatory system does not lose pressure the same way a severed human blood vessel would.
Accuracy / Caveat: Keep visuals stylised and non-graphic; avoid encouraging animal harm.

Working Title: What Is the Deepest Point on Earth?
Hook (0-2 sec): Mount Everest could fit inside this trench—with more than a mile of water still above it.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to choose Mariana Trench, Puerto Rico Trench, Java Trench or Grand Canyon.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, roughly 11 kilometres below sea level.
Core Explanation: It formed at a subduction zone where one tectonic plate bends beneath another.
Final Wow Fact: Pressure near the bottom is more than a thousand times sea-level atmospheric pressure.
Supporting Tools: Remotion depth gauge, volumetric ocean shader
Accuracy / Caveat: Depth estimates vary slightly by survey; use “about 11 km.”

Working Title: Is the Ocean Deeper Than Everest Is Tall?
Hook (0-2 sec): Put Everest at the deepest ocean point—would its summit reach the surface?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Let viewers drag Everest into Challenger Deep and predict.
Correct Answer / Reveal: No. Challenger Deep is about 11 km deep, while Everest is about 8.85 km above sea level.
Core Explanation: Even with Everest on the trench floor, more than 2 km of water would remain above the summit.
Final Wow Fact: The vertical difference is larger than many commercial aircraft fly above the ground.
Accuracy / Caveat: Use consistent reference levels and approximate surveyed values.

Working Title: What If All Earth’s Land Ice Melted?
Hook (0-2 sec): Sea level would rise by roughly 70 metres—but not overnight.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask which cities and coastlines change first on an animated globe.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Complete melting of land ice would raise global mean sea level by about 70 metres over very long timescales.
Core Explanation: Floating sea ice contributes little directly when it melts; Greenland and Antarctica contain most of the land-ice potential.
Final Wow Fact: Antarctica alone contains enough ice to raise sea level by roughly 57 metres.
Supporting Tools: Map shader, Remotion timeline and caveats
Accuracy / Caveat: Emphasise millennia-scale complete melting and avoid presenting the final map as a near-term forecast.

Working Title: Is Lightning Hotter Than the Sun?
Hook (0-2 sec): A lightning channel can be about five times hotter than the Sun’s visible surface.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to choose lightning, lava, a welding arc or the Sun’s surface.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Lightning can heat nearby air to about 30,000 C, hotter than the Sun’s roughly 5,500–5,800 C photosphere.
Core Explanation: The lightning channel is tiny and lasts only a fraction of a second; the Sun contains vastly more total energy.
Final Wow Fact: The explosive expansion of superheated air creates thunder.
Accuracy / Caveat: Compare temperature, not total heat or energy.

Working Title: Why Don’t Hurricanes Form on the Equator?
Hook (0-2 sec): The warmest ocean water is there—so why are hurricanes missing?
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the missing ingredient is heat, moisture, spin or clouds.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The Coriolis effect is essentially zero at the equator, so developing storms lack enough planetary spin to organise into a tropical cyclone.
Core Explanation: Storms typically need to form at least several degrees of latitude away, along with warm water, moisture and favourable winds.
Final Wow Fact: Cyclones rotate opposite directions in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Supporting Tools: Canvas wind particles, Remotion globe labels
Accuracy / Caveat: Coriolis is not the only formation condition; avoid saying storms can never cross the equator.

Working Title: What Was the Loudest Natural Sound Ever Recorded?
Hook (0-2 sec): People thousands of kilometres away heard the 1883 Krakatoa eruption.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer thunder, blue whale, Tunguska and Krakatoa.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The 1883 Krakatoa eruption is often described as the loudest sound in recorded history.
Core Explanation: The eruption generated enormous pressure waves that travelled around the globe multiple times; historical accounts and barometers documented them.
Final Wow Fact: The sound was heard roughly 4,800 km away, though exact “loudest” rankings depend on reconstruction and measurement.
Supporting Tools: Map wave simulation, Remotion historical cards
Accuracy / Caveat: Use “often cited” or “in recorded history”; do not present a precisely measured source-decibel number as certain.

Working Title: How Far Can Volcanic Ash Travel?
Hook (0-2 sec): Ash from one eruption can cross countries, oceans and sometimes circle the planet.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers how far the plume can go: 100 km, 1,000 km or around Earth.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Fine ash and aerosols can travel thousands of kilometres; the smallest material injected high into the atmosphere can spread globally.
Core Explanation: Travel distance depends on particle size, eruption height and wind patterns; heavy ash falls near the volcano.
Final Wow Fact: High-altitude volcanic aerosols can affect sunsets and climate far from the eruption.
Supporting Tools: Canvas particles, wind-field data, Remotion map
Accuracy / Caveat: Distinguish coarse ash from fine ash and sulfur aerosols; do not imply every eruption circles Earth.

Working Title: How Big Is the Sahara Desert?
Hook (0-2 sec): The Sahara is roughly comparable in area to China or the United States.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to place the Sahara outline over one of four countries.
Correct Answer / Reveal: At about 9.2 million square kilometres, the Sahara is close in area to China and the United States.
Core Explanation: It spans much of North Africa and includes rock plateaus, gravel plains and mountains—not only sand dunes.
Final Wow Fact: Sand seas cover only part of the Sahara; much of it is rocky or gravel desert.
Accuracy / Caveat: Area estimates vary with desert boundary definitions; use “about” and “comparable.”

Working Title: What Is Hiding Beneath Antarctica’s Ice?
Hook (0-2 sec): Beneath kilometres of ice are lakes, mountains, valleys and volcanoes.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask which feature does not exist below the ice: lakes, mountains, rivers or coral reefs.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Antarctica hides hundreds of subglacial lakes, buried mountain ranges and active geological systems.
Core Explanation: Radar, gravity and seismic measurements reveal terrain without removing the ice; liquid water can persist under pressure and geothermal heat.
Final Wow Fact: Lake Vostok lies beneath roughly 4 km of ice.
Supporting Tools: Terrain data, radar-scan shader, Remotion quiz
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid sensational claims of confirmed alien ecosystems; microbial life questions remain research topics.

Working Title: Which Country Moves About Seven Centimetres Each Year?
Hook (0-2 sec): Australia drifts northeast fast enough to affect precise GPS coordinates.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Offer India, Australia, Brazil and South Africa.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Australia moves roughly 7 cm per year with the Australian tectonic plate.
Core Explanation: Tectonic plates are constantly moving; national coordinate systems must periodically account for accumulated offset.
Final Wow Fact: Over a decade, the shift can approach the length of a forearm.
Accuracy / Caveat: Direction and rate vary across the plate and reference frame; use approximate wording.

Working Title: What Falls Faster in a Vacuum: a Bowling Ball or a Feather?
Hook (0-2 sec): Remove the air, and the feather stops losing the race.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers to predict before releasing both objects.
Correct Answer / Reveal: They fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum.
Core Explanation: Gravity gives all freely falling objects the same acceleration; air resistance creates the familiar difference on Earth.
Final Wow Fact: Apollo 15 demonstrated the effect on the Moon using a hammer and falcon feather.
Accuracy / Caveat: Release must be simultaneous and other forces negligible.

Working Title: Can Water Boil and Freeze at the Same Time?
Hook (0-2 sec): At one exact combination of pressure and temperature, solid, liquid and vapour coexist.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers whether the clip is fake, supercooled or the triple point.
Correct Answer / Reveal: At the triple point, water’s solid, liquid and gas phases can exist in equilibrium.
Core Explanation: For a precise water composition this occurs near 0.01 C and a very low pressure; “boiling and freezing” is a visual simplification of phase equilibrium.
Final Wow Fact: The water triple point was historically central to defining and realising temperature standards.
Supporting Tools: Particle phase simulation, Remotion phase diagram
Accuracy / Caveat: Use equilibrium language; do not claim ordinary water at household pressure can do this.

Working Title: Which Weighs More: a Kilogram of Steel or Feathers?
Hook (0-2 sec): The obvious answer is also the correct one—but the details get interesting.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Give viewers one second to answer before both scales settle.
Correct Answer / Reveal: They have equal mass and, in the same location, essentially equal weight: one kilogram each.
Core Explanation: The feathers occupy more volume and experience a slightly larger buoyant force from air; exact high-precision scale readings depend on how mass is calibrated.
Final Wow Fact: In a vacuum the buoyancy difference disappears.
Accuracy / Caveat: Keep the main answer simple; mention air buoyancy only as an advanced bonus.

Working Title: Can Hot Water Freeze Faster Than Cold Water?
Hook (0-2 sec): Sometimes it can—but the Mpemba effect is not a universal rule.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers which sample freezes first before running several conditions.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Under some experimental conditions, initially hotter water can freeze sooner; results depend on evaporation, convection, supercooling, container and definition of “freeze.”
Core Explanation: The effect is real in some setups but not guaranteed, and there is no single mechanism that explains every observation.
Final Wow Fact: Changing only one condition can reverse which sample freezes first.
Accuracy / Caveat: Present competing mechanisms and mixed results; never say hot water always freezes faster.

Working Title: Can Sound Really Shatter Glass?
Hook (0-2 sec): A voice can break a glass—but only if frequency, loudness and the glass all line up.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers which ingredient matters most: pitch, volume, duration or all three.
Correct Answer / Reveal: A sustained sound near the glass’s natural frequency can drive resonance; if vibration stress exceeds the material’s strength, cracks can grow and the glass can fail.
Core Explanation: The effect requires a suitable thin glass, accurate pitch and high sound level; it is not easy with ordinary speech.
Final Wow Fact: The glass vibrates before it breaks, and laser or high-speed measurements can reveal the growing amplitude.
Accuracy / Caveat: Do not encourage viewers to try unsafe high-volume experiments near glass.

Working Title: What Happens When a Magnet Falls Through a Copper Pipe?
Hook (0-2 sec): It falls in slow motion—even though copper is not a permanent magnet.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Drop a metal slug and a magnet side by side; ask which reaches the bottom first.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The magnet falls slowly because its changing magnetic field induces eddy currents in the copper, whose magnetic effect opposes the change.
Core Explanation: This is Lenz’s law. Energy is converted into a small amount of heat in the pipe.
Final Wow Fact: Cutting a slot along the pipe weakens the circulating currents and lets the magnet fall faster.
Supporting Tools: Motion Canvas field lines, Remotion timing race
Accuracy / Caveat: Copper itself is not acting as a strong permanent magnet; motion-induced currents create the braking.

Working Title: Can Light Push an Object?
Hook (0-2 sec): Light has no rest mass, yet photons can exert pressure.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether a laser can move a mirror, dust particle or spacecraft sail.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Yes. Photons carry momentum and transfer it when absorbed or reflected, creating radiation pressure.
Core Explanation: The force is tiny for everyday light but measurable; high-power lasers and solar sails can accumulate meaningful effects.
Final Wow Fact: Reflecting light transfers more momentum than absorbing the same light.
Supporting Tools: Photon particles, Motion Canvas momentum arrows
Accuracy / Caveat: Avoid visible large motion from a weak handheld laser; scale the effect honestly.

Working Title: Which Is Faster: Electricity or the Electrons?
Hook (0-2 sec): The lamp turns on almost instantly, but individual electrons drift surprisingly slowly.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask viewers whether electrons race through the wire near light speed.
Correct Answer / Reveal: The electromagnetic signal propagates through the circuit very quickly, while electron drift speed in a conductor is usually much slower.
Core Explanation: The electric field establishes along the circuit and nearby electrons respond; energy transfer is not one electron travelling from switch to bulb.
Final Wow Fact: The electrons already present throughout the wire begin moving together when the circuit is completed.
Accuracy / Caveat: Signal speed depends on cable geometry and material; avoid giving one universal fraction of light speed.

Working Title: Can Air Pressure Crush a Metal Can?
Hook (0-2 sec): Cool a little steam inside a can, and the atmosphere does the crushing.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether the can is crushed by suction, cold water, vacuum or outside air pressure.
Correct Answer / Reveal: When steam condenses, pressure inside drops; higher external atmospheric pressure collapses the can.
Core Explanation: The can is not “sucked in.” Unbalanced outside pressure pushes it inward.
Final Wow Fact: Sea-level atmosphere pushes with roughly 100,000 pascals over every exposed surface.
Accuracy / Caveat: Show as a supervised laboratory demonstration; boiling water and hot metal are hazardous.

Working Title: What If Every Atom Gained One Extra Electron?
Hook (0-2 sec): Adding one electron sounds tiny—but doing it to every atom would be catastrophic.
Viewer Interaction / Guess: Ask whether matter becomes heavier, explodes apart, turns magnetic or stays unchanged.
Correct Answer / Reveal: Matter would acquire an enormous negative charge; electrostatic repulsion and rapid electron loss would dominate, making the setup physically impossible to maintain.
Core Explanation: Many atoms cannot stably bind an extra electron, and charge would discharge into the surroundings long before a uniform state existed.
Final Wow Fact: Electrostatic forces between charged objects can vastly exceed gravity at atomic and everyday scales.
Accuracy / Caveat: Clearly label as a deliberately impossible thought experiment; do not present a literal stable scenario or a precise explosion yield.
